title: Going on the riverboat with Sun White and playing for the roustabouts
summary: Through friend Luis Andre he joined a riverboat band, washing dishes and playing excursions; he played blues on clarinet for roustabouts, and was hired at the Japanese Tea Garden because he could read.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well, a friend of mine, we went to school together, but the name was Luis Andre. Well, my brother was playing, stopped playing the violin. He was still playing the violin, but he was taking trumpet lessons, and I was taking cladid lessons, and Luis wanted to play saxophone. In other words, he was on the first one I ever played a piece on. The first piece I ever played on a saxophone, believe it or not, it was a two-land swing. It was a very first piece on, pre- and St. Philip, next to Peter Claiborne's Church. It was St. Anne's Church then. And he went on a boat with Sun White and Em, I think I was at the college end, and wanted me to go, so when he came back, he told me he didn't like the job. You know, he had just started. So when I went, I stayed on that, telling him, man, man, I think that's about three or four months, remember me?
What year was it about now?

That must have been around maybe 23, 24, maybe 21, I don't know. I was a youngster, I know, because I tell you, we didn't have nothing to do in the day at all. Sun White was washing dishes in the kitchen, and playing with the band at night. And I would be so tired, I was a youngster, just out of, you know, going to school. I was a little active. I used to go and help the rouserbots carry the stave.

No, I used to box at school in the middle of it. When I, Captain used to enjoy seeing me, you know, getting nine with them rouserbots, you know, and carry the stave. I mean, he gave me a, told everybody on the boat, anything you want to give him, any concession stand, he said, you don't pay for nothing on this boat. He said, that's a terrible youngster. And then we'd play at night, we'd play excursions from Columbia, Columbia, Mississippi, you know, and, I mean, Louisiana, and up around Arkansas. And we'd get to Cameron, Arkansas, we'd play that excursion, and then we'd turn around and come back. Well, they'd pick up freight and drop freight off on the way, you see. And at night, sometimes I'd take my clarinet and go down with them, down there by them rouserbots, because I always was a good mixer, you know, everybody was a human being, a human being to me. I would play a little blues for them, and they'd get paid off in Baton Rouge. Everybody would get paid off in Baton Rouge, you know, just give me a thousand, just give me two, baby, you know.
Just by yourself on clarinet, or?

Yeah, just by myself, just by myself. You can clarinet then? Yeah. Mm-hmm. I wasn't that great, but I mean, I could play that melody. You still need the blues. I could play that melody. Making that money, I could play that melody, you see. So I tell you, that's why Deren's Boy, and Lewis Gallo, and Bill Phillips, that's why they hired me at the Japanese Tea Garden at Melon Boy, because I could read them what I see. And they'd buy that music, and I'd read it for them, you see.
